content: The application of nitroglycerin rectal ointment should be done using the dosing line provided with the packaging to measure the appropriate length (5 mg). The ointment is applied by gently inserting a covered finger into the anal canal, no further than the first finger joint, and spreading it circumferentially. If pain prevents this, the ointment can be applied directly to the external area of the anus. It may be applied intra-anally every 12 hours until pain subsides, but treatment should not exceed three weeks. The ointment should be stored below 25°C, not frozen, and the tube must remain tightly closed. The safety and efficacy of nitroglycerin rectal ointment in individuals aged 65 years or older have not been adequately established due to insufficient clinical data. Published literature suggests that elderly patients may exhibit increased sensitivity to nitrates, which can be therapeutic but may also result in more frequent or severe hypotension, dizziness, or fainting. This increased sensitivity may be attributed to age-related declines in hepatic, renal, or cardiac function, as well as the presence of concomitant diseases or other drug therapies common in elderly populations. The use of nitroglycerin rectal ointment is contraindicated with PDE5 inhibitors (e.g., avanafil, sildenafil, tadalafil, vardenafil) due to additive vasodilation effects, which can potentiate severe hypotension. These medications should not be used within a few days of each other. Beta-blockers (e.g., acebutolol, atenolol, betaxolol, bisoprolol, carvedilol, labetalol, esmolol) can blunt the reflex tachycardia caused by nitroglycerin without preventing its hypotensive effects. When used together in patients with angina pectoris, additional hypotensive effects may occur. Caution and monitoring are advised. Calcium channel blockers (e.g., amlodipine, diltiazem, felodipine, isradipine) used concomitantly with nitroglycerin may result in marked orthostatic hypotension. Patients should be monitored for additive hypotensive effects. Diuretics (e.g., bumetanide, chlorothiazide, chlorthalidone, furosemide, hydrochlorothiazide, indapamide) and other antihypertensive agents (e.g., aliskiren, azilsartan, benazepril, candesartan, captopril, enalapril, eprosartan, fosinopril, irbesartan, hydralazine) may increase the hypotensive effects of nitroglycerin. Caution and monitoring are recommended during concomitant use. Alcohol (ethanol) can enhance the vasodilating effects of nitroglycerin, leading to additive hypotension. Alcohol consumption should be avoided during treatment. Nitroglycerin may increase the effects of aspirin and aspirin-containing products (e.g., aspirin/citric acid/sodium bicarbonate), potentially enhancing its pharmacological effects. Caution and monitoring are advised. Nitroglycerin can increase the bioavailability of ergot derivatives (e.g., dihydroergotamine, ergotamine) by reducing their first-pass metabolism. This interaction may precipitate angina pectoris or ergotism. Caution is advised when these agents are used together. Nitroglycerin may reduce the anticoagulant effects of intravenous heparin. If used concurrently, the patient’s anticoagulation status should be closely monitored. Nitroglycerin may increase the risk of methemoglobinemia when used with dapsone. Therapy should be modified, and patients should be closely monitored. In summary, nitroglycerin rectal ointment interacts with a wide range of medications, often resulting in additive hypotensive effects or altered drug metabolism. Caution, close monitoring, and in some cases, avoidance of concomitant use are necessary to ensure patient safety.
